The weird thing about my career history is that I've switched jobs and careers quite a number of times.
When I talk to many of my friends who are professionals or doctors, they're really shocked that I continue to quit jobs, start new jobs, or even hold new careers, and somehow keep getting away with it.
My wife asked me to write down a chronology of all the jobs that I've had and the odd and funny circumstances that surround the getting, having, and leaving each of those jobs. It's just so that I would be able to remember it.

# Bakground: me talk pretty one day

I think the main thing that led me down this path was my involvement in high school and university debating in the late 2000s. Competitive debating is this weird activity where you take a set of smart, nerdy, ambitious people and you train them to develop a core skill of speaking. I wasn't the very debator in the world, but I was close. I competed against teammates with the best debaters in the world, and I could beat them on any given day even if I couldn't do so consistently. I was kind of like Reggie Miller or Jimmy Butler, not a player anyone would have picked as the best of their era, but someone who could be dangerous in a playoff series. 

What debating does is wear down the gap between what you think and what you say. After a lot of painful repetition, you end up with this amazing ability to have the words that are coming out of your mouth match the ones that are in your head. This helps people become good lawyers or politicians, but the thing that I've noticed most of all is that it makes you really, really good at job interviews and meetings. 

# University jobs

The first job I ever tried to get was a summer job in Toronto in 2006. 
I went to school in Montreal that had a long distance girlfriend in Toronto and I decided that I wanted to try to move there for the summer and get some kind of job.
A lot of the people I knew who lived in Toronto moved back there in the summer and got jobs at law firms or investment banks doing research or filing. And I thought that those were easy to get.
What I didn't realize was that almost all of those people got those jobs because their parents were lawyers at those law firms. And so we're able to backfill secretarial work with university students who didn't know how to do anything.
My parents owned a cafe and bookstore, so I said about walking through the streets of Toronto, passing out resumes, looking for summer jobs.

The place I eventually found a summer job was a razor store called the Personal Edge.
The personal edge sold electric razors and other personal roaming appliances like beard trimmers, epilators, or exfoliators.
They had branched out of their core business of personal grooming to other things like watch battery replacements, knife sharpening, and the sale of various home appliances like juicers and espresso machines.
There were three mid 20s white guys who worked at the personal edge. They Listen to a lot of heavy metal music and did a lot of cocaine.
They're called cocaine hoops because their dealer worked at a sports bar called "Hoops".
I would say things like, "Yeah, I can have 10 or 20 beer if hoops are involved."
The job paid something like $5.25 an hour. And I really didn't, I never really understood how they were able to afford a cocaine habit on that wage, when I had trouble maintaining a lunch habit. 
It turned out the place was in the middle of an elaborate electric razor return scam, whereby they would fake sales of expensive electric razors, return them across the street to the Hudson Bay Company, and use the proceeds to buy cocaine.
This was eventually picked up by a Hudson Bay fraud prevention person and perpetrators were fired.

After the other employees were fired, I suddenly became one of the most important people at the largest personal edge store in southern Ontario.
I'm a regional manager, Mark Andre, made a visit to the store and noticed how coorindated my window displays were, and how well organized the air filters were, and spent a lot of time trying to get me to quit school so he could set me up with a nice little franchise in the exchange tower. I declined. 


# Millienium Research Group

In 2006, I came back to Halifax and worked in my parents' coffee shop.
I wanted to work in an office so I did what people did in 2006 to find jobs in offices, which was open Craigslist.
The only job I applied for on Craigslist was a job at a place called Millennium Research Group which did market research for medical device companies. 
I had studied philosophy in university so I didn't really have any background in any of those words, But I could talk pretty and when you're qualified for nothing, you're kind of qualified for everything so I ended up getting the job. 
Medical device market research at the time is one of the most bizarre businesses that I've never thought heard about.
In any given medical device field, there were only only about two or three companies who made any particular type of device, But they didn't really know very much about the other company's business.
So what you would do as a medical device market researcher is cold call people at these medical device companies and ask them to give you an estimate of how big the market was and how fast it was growing.
These companies would make up a number and tell it to you. You would then average those numbers and write a report about it.
The salespeople in the company would then take that report and sell it back to the companies that you had just talked to. And they would then use that report to create their future estimates of how big the market was when you called them the next time.
It was this wonderful circular business that I found very disturbing when I was working there.
Nobody was really using any actual information. We were just kind of passing here for say, back and forth between each other and paying each other to do it. 
It felt like a total scam, but now I realize that it's just how market data works. 

My particular role was to do market research on orthopedic biomaterials.
Orthopedic biometeerials are things like bone graft material and bone graft substitutes.
When you get a hip replacement or spinal fusion or something like that, they need to use some material that allows your bone to grow on to the prosthetic device.
This can be something like material that is harvested from somebody's hip and sold or can be a bone morphogenic protein which just causes the bone to grow around the prosthetic.
So all day every day I would call, I would wake up at weird times to call people all around the world and ask some questions about their thoughts on the bone market. 
Like I would come in at midnight, call a Japanese salaryman and ask him, you know, what did you think about the allopathic bone market today? You think it's gonna grow? And he would say, "Yeah!" And I would say how much do you think it's going to grow? And he would say about 5% And I would do that about four more times until I had four data points and then I would average them and write a report that said the allopathic bone market in Japan will grow about 5% next year.


## Grad school 1: Urban planning
Around the same time I was quite heartbroken about an ex-girlfriend who was really into architecture and historic preservation. And through a series of very, very bad decisions, this led me to become interested in Jane Jacobs and to quit MRG to enroll in an urban planning degree in 2007.
The urban planning degree was two years long. And so if you're keeping track of the dates here, you'll notice that I would have been graduating trying to find a job as an urban planner in 2009.
Before starting an urban degree, I didn't really think through how urban planners actually worked.
I kind of thought that they did stuff like, you know, look at nice old cities and appreciate their character. The nice old parts of cities have mostly already been planned. And urban planners spend a lot of their time working on new housing developments mostly in subburbs. If you're keeping track of the dates here, you'll notice that a two-year urban planning degree would have put me on the job market in 2009, immediately after the financial crisis stopped all new housing development for a long time. 
Most people who ended up in on the job market in 2009 had really permanent damage to their livelihoods that they never recovered from.

After three months I looked up how much money people actually made as urban planners and discovered that it was less than what I was making at MRG. 
This let me do discover the second main superpower that I've had in my career: quitting early.

I think most 21 year olds would have looked at leaving a grad program after just three months as a big waste of money.
I had already borrowed money to pay that year's tuition and if I left I wouldn't get anything out of it.
But what I knew from, but what I knew is that the main expense of going to grad school is actually the opportunity cost of working. And sinking more time into the program would actually be the bigger, would actually be the most expensive thing that I could do, so I decided to quit to find another job. 

## Bank of Montreal

In the spring of 2008, I was looking for just a replacement level professional job somewhere in Toronto.
I found a job in the part of the Bank of Montreal that manages the technology used to support the banks' trading desks.
There was this very strange executive at BMO, whose name I forget, who had a pet program to basically hire weird smart young men.
He would then have these weird smart men kind of rotate through the bank and find Until they landed into a position where they could provide some value
The idea behind this program was to basically add, I think was to basically add some randomness to their hiring process and as a philosophy studen with skills or interest in banking, technology or trading, I was certainly random.

The hiring process was a single interview with this executive. And it was one of the stranger interviews I've ever had. He asked me a number of questions and then essentially sort of looked at me for a long time, Look down at my transcripts, And then asked in a very serious tone: "So, philosophy... what is your personal opinion of the death of Socreates?" At the time I had a great fucking answer for my personal opinion on the death of Socrates and got the job.

This was again in the spring of 2008. In the time between when I signed the offer and I started, Bear Stearns went under and the financial crisis really started to accelerate. 
I remember walking around Toronto between the days that I signed the offer and when I actually started the job just getting more and more anxious that there weren't actually going to be any jobs left and this offer would be rescinded.
When I eventually did have a start date and go in, I went up to a small odd office building right next to First Canadian Place and knocked on the door.
A very confused looking secretary answered the door and said, "Gordon, I had never heard of any Gordon. I didn't think anybody was starting today. Call back later."
I was very panicked but it turns out that I just got in the start date wrong.

My job at the bank was to work for a woman named Janet Roschuck. 
Janet was a very senior and very powerful product owner, product manager at the Bank of Montreal who only worked at the bank three days a week.
She had asked for a business analyst to assist her in doing the tasks that she didn't want to do, but it turns out there was exactly one of those tasks per month.
At the end of each month, we had to send in a spreadsheet which compared the amount of hours that we had planned people would work with the amount of hours that they actually worked.
If these numbers matched, it was good news for our planning. If they didn't match, it was bad news.
My job was once a month to call all the people who submitted entries in that spreadsheet and ask them if the numbers were accurate.
If the numbers showed a large discrepancy between what we had planned to do and what we actually did, I would ask them many, many times whether they were accurate, until the numbers started matching better.
This consisted of my entire job, which really only took about five or six hours a month.
I'm really not exaggerating these numbers. I did in fact have a job which I had to go into every day, but where I really only had one solid work day per month. 
I read the entire internet, and took very long walks.
After two years of this, I decided to go to law school.

# Lawyer

I went to law school for a number of high-minded reasons. 
I wanted to understand society better. I wanted to help people. I wanted to have a career that was intellectually meaningful and stimulating.
That approximate cause was that I had a really good LSAT score that I was about to expire and I didn't want to take the test again.
I applied to two law schools, the University of Toronto and Dalhousie, and got into the wolf, and initially had accepted U of T because it was much better.
At some point I decided to sit down and do the math about how much more it would cost to go to University of Toronto versus Dalhousie and realize it was about 110,000 extra dollars, I was also filled with religious fervor and Califax was a much better place to be a Buddhist than Toronto.
So I ended up asking Delhauser to take me back and turning down U of T and moving back to Halifax.
This was probably the best decision I've ever made in my life. 
It gave me a lot of financial flexibility that I later would need to once again radically shift my career. And more and much more importantly, my future wife had also decided to try living in Halifax. 

The one big problem with law school is that I'm just really extremely lazy.
I never really cared that much about making money, but the main thing I care about is not working after 5 p.m. or on the weekends.
It turns out that almost all lawyers do in fact work a lot and this is a big part of being a lawyer.
Someone who is more thoughtful or able to self reflect better than I was at 25 probably would have known this and decided that they weren't suited for a legal career. 

To be a lawyer in Canada, you need to do one year of on-the-job training as an Articling student.
And most of your job in law school is to get good enough grades in the right sorts of classes so that you can find one of these articling positions.
Have an articling position. Your main job is to do a good enough job to get hired back as a first year lawyer,
Once you're a first year lawyer, your main job is to build enough hours to become a senior associate and maybe eventually a partner.
At some point along this career it opens up and becomes really really nice, but the first years are quite brutal.

My main criteria for an articling position was that I wanted to work in public sector law, either in a crown office or in some type of government law.
Barring that, I just wanted some type of position at kind of mid-level firm where the hours weren't too crazy.
Throughout law school I applied to maybe 200 articulating positions, Targeting public sector work or mid-level offerings with good work life balance.
I got two offers. 

The first was at a class action loss firm in Toronto with one off-putting lawyer.
The second offer was at a law firm called Lenczner Slaght Royce Smith Griffin, which was at the time and maybe is still today the very best lititation firm in Canada. 
It's hard to describe how coveted jobs at Lenczner Slaght slot were for a certain type of law student, but if you were someone who dreamed of living in the courtroom you wanted to work there, but it definitely wasn't the type of place I wanted to work. 

The way that articling works is that you have a bunch of maybe five or six students competing for two or three spots as a first year associate.
These students are also kind of pathological over achievers, so they end up working extremely long hours to try to get to the next rung in the ladder.
Since I knew it started going into it that Winston Slot and really any firm like that wasn't a place that I was ever going to be happy in the long term, I just decided at the start that I wasn't going to play that game.
I generally did a good job at the things that I was asked to do, but I didn't spend a ton of time looking for work or overdoing work to impress anybody.
I remember one good example of this. A second year associate came up to me one Friday asked me to write a memo that to me didn't look to be terribly urgent and asked me if I could have it by the end of the day.

Years after articling, I went back to Toronto for a wedding and was introduced to a few younger lawyers. 
One of them said "Wait, you're Gordon SHOTWELL? You're the guy who didn't work hard at Lenczner Slaght!"

Fundamentally though I knew that this type of law firm wasnt' for me, so when I had the opportunity to  move back to Halifax to clerk for the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal I took it. 

Clerking is its own kind of weird job. Your main task is to help judges with legal research and writing, but just as important is to kind of bring some outside perspextive into the court system. 
Judges are by nature pretty isolated from the rest of the world because the only way that they're alolowed to communicate about legal matters is through their decisions. 
Since most of what they think and care about touches legal matters in some form or another they are quite socially isolated. 
Imagine spending most of your life focused on your career, but not be allowed to talk to friends, family, or neighbours about your work. 
Imagine also that the only people you can talk to about these things are your five coworkers who never change, eventually you all just run out of stuff to talk about and get really bored. 
Clerks basically add a new smart young person to your workplace who is under the same shroud of secrecy as everyone else, and end up being a kind of buddy to an extremely smart and intimidating appellate judge. 

At this point in my career I was reasonably certain that I diddn't have the constitution for legal work and I was starting to explore working in tech and data. 

One last strange thing about clerking in Halifax. There were two regular clerks and one "Alpha clerk" who stayed over from the previous year. 
The Alpha clerk was kind of a prestige positon, and they got something like $2,000 extra dollars a year, membership in the public sector union, and the opportunity to boss around the two beta clerks. 
The position really was called "Alpha clerk".
I was given the opportunity to be the alphas clerk, but declined to seek my fortune in the tech world.
